old: A psalm of David, which he sang to the Lord concerning the words of Cush, son of Jemini.
new: A psalm of David, which he sang to the Lord concerning the words of Chusi, son of Jemini.
reason: The name is Latin "Chusi"; the English "Cush" gives the Hebrew form instead of this Latin.

old: Let the wickedness of sinners come to an end, and You will guide the just, God, who searches hearts and kidneys.
new: The wickedness of sinners will come to an end, and You will guide the just, God, who searches hearts and kidneys.
reason: Latin "Consumetur" is future indicative, a statement; the English "Let ... come to an end" turns it into a wish.

old: his departure is from the height of heaven, and his meeting place is at its height. No one can hide from his heat.
new: his departure is from the height of heaven, and his circuit reaches to its height. No one can hide from his heat.
reason: Latin "occursus ejus usque ad summum ejus" means his course runs as far as its height; "his meeting place is at its height" misrenders "occursus" and drops "usque ad".

old: May the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart always be pleasing in Your sight, Lord, my helper and my redeemer.
new: The words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart will always be pleasing in Your sight, Lord, my helper and my redeemer.
reason: Latin "Et erunt ut complaceant" is a future statement (they will be pleasing); the English "May ... be pleasing" turns it into a wish.

old: May your hand find all your enemies; may your right hand find all who hate you.
new: May your hand be found by all your enemies; may your right hand find all who hate you.
reason: Latin "Inveniatur manus tua omnibus inimicis tuis" is passive (may your hand be found by your enemies); the English made the hand the finder.

old: In a place of pasture, there He has set me. Beside refreshing water He has led me;
new: In a place of pasture, there He has set me. Beside refreshing water He has nourished me;
reason: Latin "educavit me" (from educare) means He has brought me up or nourished me, not "led".

old: For they have not understood the Lord's works, and by the works of His hands You will destroy them and not build them up.
new: For they have not understood the Lord's works and the works of His hands; You will destroy them and not build them up.
reason: Latin "et in opera manuum ejus" continues what they did not understand; the English "by the works of His hands You will destroy" made it God's instrument.

old: The Lord is the strength of His people and the protector of the victories of His anointed.
new: The Lord is the strength of His people and the protector of the deliverances of His anointed.
reason: Latin "salvationum" means deliverances or saving acts, not "victories".

old: Let them not say in their hearts, “Aha, aha! Just as we wanted!” Nor let them say, “We have devoured him.”
new: Let them not say in their hearts, “Aha, aha, for our soul!” Nor let them say, “We have devoured him.”
reason: English 'Just as we wanted!' renders the Hebrew idiom; the Latin has 'animae nostrae', 'for our soul'.

old: I spoke with my tongue: “Make my end known to me, Lord, and what the number of my days is, so that I may know what remains for me.
new: I spoke with my tongue: “Make my end known to me, Lord, and what the number of my days is, so that I may know what is lacking to me.
reason: English 'what remains for me' does not render Latin 'quid desit mihi', what is lacking to me.

old: You are my King and my God, who commands victories for Jacob.
new: You are my King and my God, who commands deliverances for Jacob.
reason: English 'victories' renders the Hebrew sense; Latin 'salutes' means deliverances or salvations.

old: Go around Zion and encircle it; tell of its towers.
new: Go around Zion and encircle it; tell in its towers.
reason: English 'tell of its towers' changes Latin 'narrate in turribus ejus', recount in its towers.

old: Set your hearts upon its strength and distinguish its houses, so that you may recount it to another generation.
new: Set your hearts upon its strength and distribute its houses, so that you may recount it to another generation.
reason: English 'distinguish' mistranslates Latin 'distribuite', distribute or divide.

old: See, they will speak with their mouth, and a sword is on their lips, for they say, “Who has heard?”
new: See, they will speak with their mouth, and a sword is on their lips, for who has heard?
reason: The English added "they say", assigning the question to the enemies; the Latin "quoniam quis audivit?" has no verb of saying.

old: God will show me triumph over my enemies. Do not kill them, lest my peoples forget. Scatter them in Your strength and bring them down, my protector, Lord:
new: God will show me over my enemies. Do not kill them, lest my peoples forget. Scatter them in Your strength and bring them down, my protector, Lord:
reason: The English added "triumph"; the Latin "Deus ostendet mihi super inimicos meos" has no such noun, only God showing the speaker something over or concerning his enemies.

old: Let them not say among the nations, “Where is their God?” Let vengeance for the outpoured blood of Your servants become known among the nations before our eyes.
new: Lest they say among the nations, “Where is their God?” Let vengeance for the outpoured blood of Your servants become known among the nations before our eyes.
reason: Latin "Ne forte dicant" is a purpose clause, lest they say, continuing the prayer; the English turned it into a wish, let them not say.

old: We will not depart from You. You will give us life, and we will call upon Your name.
new: We do not depart from You. You will give us life, and we will call upon Your name.
reason: Latin "non discedimus" is present tense, we do not depart; the English made it future, we will not depart.

old: The dwelling of all who rejoice is as though in you.
new: The dwelling in you is as of all who rejoice.
reason: Latin "Sicut laetantium omnium habitatio est in te" says the dwelling in you is as of all who rejoice; the English made the rejoicers' dwelling only 'as though' in Zion.

old: Bless the Lord, all His angels, mighty in strength, doing His word as you hear the voice of His sayings.
new: Bless the Lord, all His angels, mighty in strength, doing His word in order to hear the voice of His sayings.
reason: Latin "ad audiendam vocem" is a purpose phrase (in order to hear); the English "as you hear" made it a temporal clause.

old: Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel, from age to age, and let all the people say, “Let it be, let it be.”
new: Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel, from age to age, and all the people will say, “Let it be, let it be.”
reason: Latin 'et dicet omnis populus' is a future statement, 'and all the people will say', not a command 'let all the people say'.

old: because they had embittered God's sayings and made void the counsel of the Most High.
new: because they had embittered God's sayings and provoked the counsel of the Most High.
reason: Latin 'irritaverunt' means 'provoked', not 'made void'.

old: Happy is the man who shows mercy and lends; he will order his words with judgment,
new: Pleasing is the man who shows mercy and lends; he will order his words with judgment,
reason: Latin 'jucundus' means pleasing or agreeable, not 'happy'.

old: and in Your mercy You will scatter my enemies and destroy all who afflict my soul, for I am Your servant.
new: and in Your mercy You will wipe out my enemies and destroy all who afflict my soul, for I am Your servant.
reason: Latin 'disperdes' means 'destroy utterly', not 'scatter'.

old: The Lord guards all who love Him, and will scatter all sinners.
new: The Lord guards all who love Him, and will destroy all sinners.
reason: Latin 'disperdet' means 'will destroy utterly', not 'will scatter'.

old: The Lord guards foreigners; He will uphold the orphan and the widow, and scatter the ways of sinners.
new: The Lord guards foreigners; He will uphold the orphan and the widow, and destroy the ways of sinners.
reason: Latin 'disperdet' means 'will destroy utterly', not 'will scatter'.

old: who leaves the companion of her youth
new: who leaves the guide of her youth
reason: Latin "ducem pubertatis suae" means the guide (leader) of her youth; "companion" renders the Hebrew rather than this Latin.

old: A slack hand has produced want, but the hand of the diligent prepares riches. Whoever relies on lies feeds the winds; that same person chases flying birds.
new: A slack hand has produced want, but the hand of the strong prepares riches. Whoever relies on lies feeds the winds; that same person chases flying birds.
reason: Latin "manus fortium" means "the hand of the strong," not "the hand of the diligent" (the Hebrew sense).

old: The hand of the diligent will rule, but the slack hand will serve under tribute.
new: The hand of the strong will rule, but the slack hand will serve under tribute.
reason: Latin "manus fortium" means "the hand of the strong," not "the hand of the diligent" (the Hebrew sense).

old: [Chorus] Where has your beloved gone, most beautiful among women? Where has your beloved turned aside, so that we may seek him with you?
new: [Chorus] Where has your beloved gone, most beautiful among women? Where has your beloved turned aside? And we will seek him with you.
reason: Latin "et quæremus eum tecum" is a future statement (and we will seek him with you), not a purpose clause "so that we may seek".
